label: rem:scope
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:scope}
No smallness assumption is imposed on the initial data.
The weak-existence theorem alone does not assert a pointwise upper or positive lower
bound for the limiting density, uniqueness of general weak
solutions, or global existence of strong solutions.
Strong continuity in a given finite \(L^p\) space uses a higher
fixed moment; no estimate uniform as \(p\to\infty\) is involved.
The starting times in \eqref{eq:energy-start} are not enlarged
to all times, and no global energy equality is claimed.
The proof treats the full interval $\beta>1$ directly. With
$B=\max\{\beta,2\}$, the density-moment exponent in
\eqref{uni:sublinear-ode} remains strictly below one.
The fixed-parameter closure \eqref{fix:density-closure} compares
the powers $1+3B/8$ and $(B+2)/3$ with $B$; both are strictly
smaller because $B\ge2$. Thus the artificial quadratic viscosity
controls the lower-$\beta$ range, while the original viscosity
supplies the dominant power when $\beta>2$.
The bounded multipliers in \eqref{comp:quotient-sources} require
only $\beta>1$. In particular, $\beta=4/3$ and $\beta=2$ are
included in the weak theorem, without endpoint limiting arguments.

label: thm:weak-strong
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:weak-strong}
Let $\beta>1$ and $\gamma>1$.
Suppose $(\rho,u,H)$ is a finite-energy renormalized weak solution in
Definition~\ref{def:weak}, and $(r,U,B)$ solves the same equations in
\eqref{eq:strong-class}. If their initial density, momentum, and magnetic
field agree, the solutions coincide on $[0,T]$.

label: rem:strong-scope
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:strong-scope}
The number $R$ is arbitrary and is fixed before $m$ is chosen. Thus the
velocity and magnetic norms need not be small. For $\gamma>3$, however,
\eqref{eq:scaled-data} requires an absolutely small density perturbation,
$\|\rho_0-m\|_{H^2}\le Rm^{-(\gamma-3)/2}$; the absence of an upper
bound on $\gamma$ must not be separated from this hypothesis.
For $\gamma<3$ the same condition even allows an additive density
perturbation of order $m^{(3-\gamma)/2}$, which is still small relative
to $m$. Nonzero mean magnetic fields are allowed.

In particular, for fixed $r_0,u_0,H_0\in H^2$ with $\int r_0=0$,
$\operatorname{div} H_0=0$, and $\rho_0=m+r_0$, the theorem applies when
\begin{equation}\label{eq:fixed-additive-range}
 1<\beta<2,\qquad \Gamma_*(\beta)<\gamma\le3.
\end{equation}
If $r_0=0$, it applies to every $\gamma>\Gamma_*(\beta)$.
The lower threshold is $5-2\beta$ for $1<\beta\le4/3$ and
$\beta+1$ for $\beta\ge4/3$.
Its minimum is $7/3$, attained at $\beta=4/3$, but the theorem does not
include equality. For example, $\beta=33/25$ and $\gamma=12/5$ satisfy
both $\beta<4/3$ and $\gamma<5/2$. These are sufficient conditions from the present
estimates, not claimed necessary or optimal conditions for the equations.
Figure~\ref{fig:parameter-regions} summarizes these parameter ranges,
with $\gamma$ on the horizontal axis and $\beta$ on the vertical axis.

label: pre:weighted-poincare
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Weighted Poincar\'e inequality

title: Proof
body_md:
Writing \(M=\int\rho\), we have
\[
 M\lvert \langle v\rangle\rvert
 \le \lvert \int\rho v\,\mathrm dx\rvert
       +\lvert \int\rho(v-\langle v\rangle)\,\mathrm dx\rvert
 \le \sqrt M\lVert \sqrt\rho\,v\rVert_2
       +\lVert \rho\rVert_\kappa\lVert v-\langle v\rangle\rVert_{\kappa'}.
\]
Since \(\kappa'<\infty\), \eqref{pre:sobolev} controls the last norm.
Another application of \eqref{pre:sobolev} proves the assertion.

label: pre:friedrichs
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Friedrichs commutator in conservative form

title: Proof
body_md:
In the distributional convolution formula,
\[
 c_\ell(x)=z_\ell(x)\operatorname{div} u(x)
 +\int\nabla J_\ell(h)\cdot
             \bigl(u(x)-u(x-h)\bigr)z(x-h)\,\mathrm d h.
\]
The fundamental theorem of calculus and H\"older's inequality give
the stated uniform bound. For smooth \(u\), spatial translation
continuity of \(z\) shows that the integral converges to
\(-z\operatorname{div} u\), whereas the first term converges to \(z\operatorname{div} u\).
Their sum therefore converges to zero in \(L^2_tL^r_x\).
Approximation of \(u\) in \(L^2_tH^1_x\), followed by the uniform
bound, proves \eqref{pre:friedrichs-est}. This is the commutator
underlying renormalization \cite{DiPernaLions1989}. It concerns fixed
limiting functions \(z,u\), not strong convergence between distinct
approximate solutions.

label: pre:wente
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Periodic Jacobian pairing

title: Proof
body_md:
The periodic Wente estimate, equivalently the Hardy-space
Jacobian estimate \cite{CLMS1993}, gives
\[
 \lVert \nabla(-\Delta)^{-1}\det\nabla v\rVert_2
 \le C\lVert \nabla v_1\rVert_2\lVert \nabla v_2\rVert_2.
\]
The Jacobian has zero mean. Integration by parts against
\(\phi-\langle \phi\rangle\) proves \eqref{pre:wente-est}.

label: pre:bkm
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Logarithmic div--curl estimate

title: Proof
body_md:
A periodic dyadic decomposition and the div--curl representation
of \(\nabla v\) give, for every integer \(N\ge1\),
\[
 \lVert \nabla v\rVert_\infty
 \le C\lVert \nabla v\rVert_2
   +CN\bigl(\lVert \operatorname{div} v\rVert_\infty+\lVert \operatorname{curl} v\rVert_\infty\bigr)
   +C_q2^{-N(1-2/q)}\lVert \nabla^2v\rVert_q.
\]
The finite low-frequency block is controlled by Bernstein's
inequality. Each intermediate block is a uniformly bounded
localized multiplier applied to \(\operatorname{div} v,\operatorname{curl} v\); the last term
follows from Bernstein's inequality and summation of the high
frequencies. Choose \(N\) comparable to
\(1+(1-2/q)^{-1}\log(e+\lVert \nabla^2v\rVert_q)\).

\label{uni:strong-solution-tests}
The preceding identities also hold on compact subintervals for
positive-density strong solutions satisfying
\(\rho,u,H\in C_tH^2_x\), \(u_t,H_t\in L^2_tH^1_x\), and
\(\rho_t\in C_tH^1_x\). In fact
\((\rho u)_t\in L^2_tH^1_x\), so that
\(\xi_t\in L^2_tH^2_x\) and
\(\partial_t(\Lambda_\delta(\rho)-\xi)\in L^2_tH^1_x\).
The positive-part integral is therefore absolutely continuous,
and its chain rule follows by smooth approximation of the
positive part. Magnetic power tests are justified in the same
way. The individual density bounds needed for these chain rules
do not enter the estimates above.
The present argument neither constructs the approximate solutions
globally nor proves that the additional dissipation
\(\delta\int\rho^2d^2\) tends to zero. It supplies uniform finite
moments and the vanishing stress \eqref{uni:small-stress-est}.

label: fix:linear
title: Proof
body_md:
We give the construction and the estimates needed for the continuation
argument. For a prescribed density \(r\), write
\[
 \mathcal L_r z=\mu\Delta z+
       \nabla\bigl((\mu+\lambda_\delta(r))\operatorname{div} z\bigr).
\]
First consider
\begin{equation}\label{fix:linear}
 r z_t-\mathcal L_r z=f,\qquad
 c\le r\le C,\qquad
 \sup_t(\|r\|_{H^2}+\|r_t\|_{H^1})\le N.
\end{equation}
Let \(P_m\) be a symmetric Fourier projection. The finite-dimensional
mass matrix is positive definite. Its inverse also has the following
bound, uniform in \(m\):
\begin{equation}\label{fix:mass-inverse}
 P_m(rq)=P_m g,\quad q=P_mq
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 \|q\|_2\le c^{-1}\|g\|_2,\qquad
 \|q\|_{H^1}\le C_N\|g\|_{H^1}.
\end{equation}
Indeed, testing successively with \(q\) and \((1-\Delta)q\) leaves only
the additional term \(\int\nabla r\cdot\nabla q\,q\). It satisfies
\[
 \left|\int\nabla r\cdot\nabla q\,q\right|
 \le C_N\|q\|_2^{1/2}\|q\|_{H^1}^{3/2}
 \le\varepsilon\|q\|_{H^1}^2+C_{N,\varepsilon}\|q\|_2^2.
\]
Applied to the projected equation, this gives
\begin{equation}\label{fix:linear-time}
 \|z_{m,t}\|_{H^1}
 \le C_N\bigl(\|z_m\|_{H^3}+\|f\|_{H^1}\bigr).
\end{equation}
Here \(\|\mathcal L_r z\|_{H^1}\le C_N\|z\|_{H^3}\);
the coefficient terms use \(L^4\times L^4\) and \(L^2\times L^\infty\).

Testing the projected equation with \(z+\Delta^2z\) retains the weighted
inertia. Its highest-order part is exactly
\begin{equation}\label{fix:inertial-identity}
 \int rz_t\Delta^2z
 =\frac12\frac d{dt}\int r|\Delta z|^2
       -\frac12\int r_t|\Delta z|^2
 +2\int(\nabla r\cdot\nabla z_t)\Delta z
       +\int(\Delta r)z_t\Delta z .
\end{equation}
Put \(Z_j=\|z\|_{H^j}\). The last two terms are bounded, by
\eqref{fix:linear-time}, by
\[
 C_N(Z_3+\|f\|_{H^1})Z_2^{1/2}Z_3^{1/2}
 \le\varepsilon Z_3^2+
       C_{N,\varepsilon}(Z_2^2+\|f\|_{H^1}^2).
\]
The \(r_t\) term is bounded by \(C_NZ_2Z_3\).
For \(b=\mu+\lambda_\delta(r)\) and \(d_z=\operatorname{div} z\), the other
highest-order contribution is
\[
 \int b|\Delta d_z|^2+
 \int\bigl(2\nabla b\cdot\nabla d_z+(\Delta b)d_z\bigr)\Delta d_z.
\]
Its second integral is bounded by \(C_NZ_2^{1/2}Z_3^{3/2}\).
The shear term supplies \(\mu\|\nabla\Delta z\|_2^2\).
The forcing requires only \(H^1\), since
\(\int f\Delta^2z=-\int\nabla f\cdot\nabla\Delta z\).
Together with the zeroth-order estimate, this proves
\begin{equation}\label{fix:linear-H2}
 \mathcal E_2'+c_N Z_3^2
 \le C_N\mathcal E_2+C_N\|f\|_{H^1}^2,\qquad
 \mathcal E_2=\int r(|z|^2+|\Delta z|^2)\asymp Z_2^2.
\end{equation}
The energy-equivalence constants depend on the density interval, not on
its \(H^2\) norm. The same argument with \(z-\Delta z\), using first the
\(L^2\) part of \eqref{fix:mass-inverse}, proves
\begin{equation}\label{fix:linear-H1}
 \mathcal E_1'+c_N\|z\|_{H^2}^2
 \le C_N\mathcal E_1+C_N\|f\|_2^2,\qquad
 \mathcal E_1=\int r(|z|^2+|\nabla z|^2).
\end{equation}
Galerkin compactness gives the linear solution; the same energy
estimates give its uniqueness.

Start with heat extensions \(u^0,H^0\) of the initial data and iterate
\begin{equation}\label{fix:iteration}
 \begin{aligned}
 &\rho^{n+1}_t+\operatorname{div}(\rho^{n+1}u^n)=0,\\
 &\rho^{n+1}u^{n+1}_t-\mathcal L_{\rho^{n+1}}u^{n+1}=f^n,\\
 &f^n=-\rho^{n+1}u^n\cdot\nabla u^n-\nabla P(\rho^{n+1})
                      +\operatorname{div}\mathbb M(H^n),\\
 &H^{n+1}_t-\nu\Delta H^{n+1}
       =\operatorname{div}(u^n\otimes H^n-H^n\otimes u^n).
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
All iterates have the prescribed initial data. The last tensor is
antisymmetric, so its double divergence vanishes and
\(\operatorname{div} H^{n+1}=0\).
On a fixed \(H^2\) ball, the two parabolic right-hand sides are bounded
in \(L^\infty H^1\). The transport estimates give
\begin{equation}\label{fix:transport-ball}
 \begin{aligned}
 \|\rho^{n+1}\|_{L^\infty(0,t;H^2)}
 &\le\|\rho_0\|_{H^2}
          \exp\bigl(C\sqrt t\,\|u^n\|_{L^2(0,t;H^3)}\bigr),\\
 \|\rho_t^{n+1}\|_{L^\infty(0,t;H^1)}&\le C_N .
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
The characteristic formula keeps the density in
\([c_0/2,2C_0]\) after reducing \(t\).
Choose first an \(H^2\) ball with strict margin over the initial weighted
energies, then a ball for the \(L^2H^3\) norms, and finally a small time.
In \eqref{fix:linear-H2} the initial energy is multiplied by a Gronwall
factor that can be kept below \(2\); after absorption the shear and
magnetic dissipation retain fixed positive coefficients.
Consequently this order of choices preserves both balls.
It also bounds \(u_t^n,H_t^n\) in \(L^2H^1\).

For completeness, the contraction does not require the entire
\(L^2H^3\) norm of the initial heat layer to be small.
Write \(R^{n+1}=\rho^{n+1}-\rho^n\), \(U^{n+1}=u^{n+1}-u^n\),
and \(Z^{n+1}=H^{n+1}-H^n\). Since
\[
 R^{n+1}_t+\operatorname{div}(u^nR^{n+1})
       =-\operatorname{div}(\rho^n U^n),\qquad R^{n+1}(0)=0,
\]
the \(H^1\) transport estimate implies
\begin{equation}\label{fix:density-difference}
 \|R^{n+1}\|_{L^\infty H^1}^2
       \le Ct\|U^n\|_{L^2H^2}^2.
\end{equation}
The velocity difference has the new density as its inertia coefficient,
and its additional source terms are
\[
 -R^{n+1}u_t^n+
 \nabla\bigl((\lambda_\delta(\rho^{n+1})
                 -\lambda_\delta(\rho^n))\operatorname{div} u^n\bigr).
\]
Their \(L^2\) norm is bounded by
\[
 C\|R^{n+1}\|_{H^1}
                  (\|u_t^n\|_{H^1}+\|u^n\|_{H^3}).
\]
For example, the differentiated coefficient terms use respectively
\(L^2\times L^\infty\), \(L^4\times L^4\times L^\infty\), and
\(L^4\times L^4\), not an \(H^1\)-to-\(L^\infty\) embedding.
The differences of the remaining sources are bounded in \(L^2\) by
\(C(\|R^{n+1}\|_{H^1}+\|U^n\|_{H^1}+\|Z^n\|_{H^1})\).
Thus \eqref{fix:linear-H1} and \eqref{fix:density-difference} give
\(\mathfrak D_{n+1}\le Ct\mathfrak D_n\), where
\(\mathfrak D_n\) is the squared \(L^\infty H^1\cap L^2H^2\)
difference norm of \(u^n,H^n\).
The small factor is the time integral in
\eqref{fix:density-difference}. Contraction, weak compactness in the
higher norms, and the equations give \eqref{fix:local-class}.
Strong \(H^2\) continuity follows from the linear energy identities
and the \(H^2\) transport estimate. The same difference argument proves
uniqueness and the asserted uniform restart time.

label: fix:global
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{fix:global}
For every fixed \(0<\delta\le1\), every positive-density \(H^2\)
initial datum with \(\operatorname{div} H_0=0\) generates a unique global solution
in the local class \eqref{fix:local-class} on every finite time interval.
The density remains bounded above and away from zero on such intervals,
with bounds allowed to depend on \(\delta\) and the initial data.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let \(T_*\) be the maximal local existence time.
If \(T_*<\infty\), fix \(T>T_*\) and apply all the preceding estimates
on \([0,\tau]\), \(\tau<T_*\).
The uniform moment bounds hold on each such interval with constants
independent of \(\tau\).
The logarithmic energy estimate and
\eqref{fix:density-closure} first give the common positive density
interval \eqref{fix:density-interval}.
Equations \eqref{fix:bounded-low-energy} and
\eqref{fix:continuation-bounds} then give a common \(H^2\) ball.
For any sequence \(t_j\uparrow T_*\), Proposition~\ref{fix:local}
therefore provides the same positive lower bound for the restart
lifetime at \(t_j\). Restarting and using local uniqueness extends the
solution beyond \(T_*\), a contradiction.
This does not require first constructing a strong \(H^2\) limit at
the terminal time. Hence \(T_*=\infty\).

label: comp:flux
title: Lemma
head: environment

label: comp:b-continuity
title: Proof
body_md:
Put $b_n=b(\rho_n)$ and $K_n=k_b(\rho_n)d_n$. The exact nonlinear
continuity equation is
\begin{equation}\label{comp:b-continuity}
 \partial_tb_n+\operatorname{div}(b_nu_n)=-K_n.
\end{equation}
In view of \eqref{comp:b-condition}, $K_n$ is bounded in $L^2(Q_T)$.
Hence $b_n$ is compact in $L^2H^{-\eta}$ for $0<\eta<1$. The argument
in \eqref{comp:product-identification} gives
$b_nu_n\rightharpoonup\overline b\,u$ in $L^2L^2$. Writing
$K_n\rightharpoonup\overline K$ in $L^2(Q_T)$, we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{comp:b-limit}
 \partial_t\overline b+\operatorname{div}(\overline b\,u)=-\overline K.
\end{equation}
Neither $\overline b=b(\rho)$ nor
$\overline K=k_b(\rho)\operatorname{div} u$ is used here.

Let $\Delta^{-1}$ be the inverse of the negative-spectrum Laplacian on
mean-zero functions, with its zero mode set to zero, and define
\begin{equation}\label{comp:potential}
 \Phi_n=\Delta^{-1}\operatorname{div} m_n,\qquad
 \mathcal R_{ij}=\partial_i\partial_j\Delta^{-1}.
\end{equation}
The multiplier $\mathcal R_{ij}$ is self-adjoint and has symbol
$\xi_i\xi_j/|\xi|^2$ at nonzero frequencies. The order $-1$ of the
potential, together with \eqref{comp:strong-negative}, gives
\begin{equation}\label{comp:potential-compactness}
\begin{aligned}
 &\Phi_n\to\Phi\quad\text{in }L^2H^{2/5}\subset L^2L^2,\\
 &\Phi_n\text{ bounded in }L^\infty W^{1,4/3},\qquad
   \partial_t\Phi_n\text{ bounded in }L^2L^{8/7}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

Fix $\psi\in C_c^\infty(Q_T)$ and set
\begin{equation}\label{comp:commutator-definition}
 C_{n,i}=\sum_j[u_{n,j},\mathcal R_{ij}](\psi b_n),\qquad
 [v,\mathcal R]f=v\mathcal Rf-\mathcal R(vf).
\end{equation}
The nonendpoint derivative commutator estimate
of \cite{CoifmanMeyer1978} gives
\begin{equation}\label{comp:commutator-bound}
 \lVert \nabla[v,\mathcal R_{ij}]f\rVert_{3/2}
       \le C\lVert \nabla v\rVert_2\lVert f\rVert_6.
\end{equation}
The zero-order term is controlled by H\"older's inequality and the
$L^q$ boundedness of $\mathcal R_{ij}$. Thus $C_n$ is bounded in
$L^2W^{1,3/2}\hookrightarrow L^2H^{3/5}$. No derivative of $b_n$ is
required. Strong negative-space convergence of $b_n$ identifies both
products in \eqref{comp:commutator-definition}, so
\begin{equation}\label{comp:commutator-limit}
\begin{aligned}
 C_n&\rightharpoonup C\quad\text{in }L^2H^{3/5},\\
 C_i&=\sum_j[u_j,\mathcal R_{ij}](\psi\overline b),\qquad
 \int_0^T\langle m_n,C_n\rangle\,\mathrm dt\longrightarrow
       \int_0^T\langle m,C\rangle\,\mathrm dt.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
For instance, testing $u_n\mathcal R(\psi b_n)$ transfers the difference
$b_n-\overline b$ to a strong $H^{-\eta}$ factor paired with a bounded
$H^1$ factor. The last convergence in \eqref{comp:commutator-limit}
uses \eqref{comp:strong-negative}, not strong convergence of $C_n$.

Define the magnetic potential
\begin{equation}\label{comp:magnetic-potential}
 \mathcal A_n=M_n-\langle M_n\rangle
                    -\sum_{i,j}\mathcal R_{ij}(H_{n,i}H_{n,j}).
\end{equation}
It converges strongly in $L^1L^2$ by
\eqref{comp:magnetic-compactness}. Applying $\Delta^{-1}\operatorname{div}$ to the
momentum equation yields the exact identity
\begin{equation}\label{comp:potential-equation}
\begin{aligned}
 \partial_t\Phi_n+\mathcal R_{ij}(m_{n,i}u_{n,j})+\mathcal A_n
       &=-F_n+\langle F_n\rangle
     +e_n-\langle e_n\rangle,
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
where repeated indices are summed. Testing with $\psi b_n$, integrating
in time by means of \eqref{comp:b-continuity}, and using self-adjointness
of $\mathcal R_{ij}$ give
\begin{equation}\label{comp:localized-identity}
\begin{aligned}
 \int_{Q_T}\psi b_nF_n
 ={}&\int_{Q_T}\bigl[\Phi_nb_n(\psi_t+u_n\cdot\nabla\psi)
                    -m_n\cdot C_n-\psi\Phi_nK_n\bigr]\\
    &+\int_{Q_T}\psi b_n(e_n-\langle e_n\rangle-\mathcal A_n)
       +\int_0^T\langle F_n\rangle\Big(\int_{\mathbb T^2}\psi b_n\,\mathrm dx\Big)\,\mathrm dt.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Here and in similar formulas the unmarked space-time integrals use
$\,\mathrm dx\,\mathrm dt$. In particular, the source term has the negative sign displayed
in \eqref{comp:localized-identity}. The commutator sign follows from
$\partial_j\Phi_n=\mathcal R_{ij}m_{n,i}$.

Every contribution in \eqref{comp:localized-identity} has a justified limit.
The time-cutoff and transport terms use strong $\Phi_n$ in $L^2L^2$
and weak convergence of $b_n$ and $b_nu_n$. The commutator term uses
\eqref{comp:commutator-limit}. Crucially, the actual source converges to
$-\int_{Q_T}\psi\Phi\overline K$, by strong $\Phi_n$ and weak $K_n$ in
$L^2(Q_T)$. The magnetic term uses strong $L^1L^2$ convergence of
$\mathcal A_n$ and the uniform bound for $b_n$.

The mean term requires a separate time compactness argument. The function
$B_{n,\psi}(t)=\int_{\mathbb T^2}\psi b_n\,\mathrm dx$ satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{comp:mean-time}
 B_{n,\psi}'=\int_{\mathbb T^2}
       (\psi_tb_n+\nabla\psi\cdot b_nu_n-\psi K_n)\,\mathrm dx.
\end{equation}
It is bounded in $H^1(0,T)$ and therefore converges strongly in
$C([0,T])$ along a subsequence. This is sufficient to pair it with the
weak $L^2$ limit of $\langle F_n\rangle$. Finally, the artificial-stress contribution
$\int_{Q_T}\psi b_n(e_n-\langle e_n\rangle)$ vanishes by \eqref{comp:small-stress}.

To identify the resulting expression, one must also justify the time
integration by parts at the limit. The appropriate spaces are
\begin{equation}\label{comp:limit-time-spaces}
\begin{aligned}
 &\Phi\in L^2W^{1,8/7},\qquad \Phi_t\in L^2L^{8/7},\\
 &\overline b\in L^2L^8,\qquad
       \overline b_t\in L^2W^{-1,8}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Indeed, $\overline b u\in L^2L^8$ and $\overline K\in L^2L^2$; moreover,
$L^2\hookrightarrow W^{-1,8}$ is dual to
$W^{1,8/7}\hookrightarrow L^2$. Regularizing the fixed limit functions
in these dual spaces proves
\begin{equation}\label{comp:limit-time-product}
 -\int_{Q_T}\psi\overline b\Phi_t
 =\int_{Q_T}\bigl[\Phi\overline b(\psi_t+u\cdot\nabla\psi)
       +\psi\overline b u\cdot\nabla\Phi-\psi\Phi\overline K\bigr].
\end{equation}
The spatial products are integrable since
$u\cdot\nabla\Phi\in L^2L^{8/7}$ and
$\Phi\overline K\in L^2L^{4/3}$. No $L^2H^1$ estimate for $\Phi$ is
being assumed. Apply \eqref{comp:limit-time-product} to the limit of
\eqref{comp:potential-equation}. It reproduces precisely the limit of
the right-hand side of \eqref{comp:localized-identity}, including the
same term $-\int\psi\Phi\overline K$. The result is
$\int\psi\overline F\,\overline b$, proving
\eqref{comp:flux-factorization}. A countable dense family of tests,
followed by the uniform bounds, provides a common subsequence.

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $R=\langle z\rangle_{\mathsf N}>0$ and
$\mathcal H(z\mid R)=z\log(z/R)-z+R$. On $R/2\le z\le2R$,
$|k(z)-k(R)|\le2L_k|z-R|/R$ and
$\mathcal H(z\mid R)\ge|z-R|^2/(4R)$. On $z\ge2R$, respectively
$z\le R/2$, the relative entropy bounds a fixed positive multiple of
$z$, respectively $R$. Boundedness of $k$ then proves
$|(z-R)(k(z)-k(R))|\le C(\lVert k\rVert_\infty+L_k)\mathcal H(z\mid R)$.
Taking expectations proves the assertion. If $R=0$, use
\eqref{comp:vacuum}.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
All weak compactness statements were obtained before density identification.
The preceding argument applies to the same subsequence and proves
\eqref{comp:defect-zero}. Strict convexity of $z\log z$ on $[0,\infty)$
now yields $\mathsf N_{t,x}=\delta_{\rho(t,x)}$ almost everywhere.
Thus $\rho_n\to\rho$ in measure. For each fixed finite $k$, a higher
moment in \eqref{comp:moments} gives uniform integrability of
$|\rho_n-\rho|^k$. Vitali's theorem proves \eqref{comp:conclusion}, and
the same reasoning applies to each fixed power of the density.

In particular, $\rho_n^\beta\to\rho^\beta$ strongly in $L^2(Q_T)$.
Pairing this with weak $d_n\to d$ in $L^2(Q_T)$ identifies the bulk
stress in distributions. Likewise, the uniform $L^2$ bound for
$\rho_n^{\beta/2}d_n$ and the strong convergence of
$\rho_n^{\beta/2}$ identify its weak $L^2$ limit as
$\rho^{\beta/2}d$. This proves \eqref{comp:stress-conclusion}.
head: environment

label: comp:dissipation-remark
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{comp:dissipation-remark}
The proof establishes strong density compactness and identifies the
original constitutive stress. It does not require, or assert, strong
convergence of the velocity gradients or disappearance of
$\delta_n\rho_n^2d_n^2$. That nonnegative dissipation can be discarded
when passing to the energy inequality. The exact continuity equation,
and hence the absence of a measure source in
\eqref{comp:defect-equation}, is essential to the argument given here.

label: as:kinetic
title: Proposition
head: environment
name: Weighted kinetic compactness

title: Proof
body_md:
Let \(v_n=\sqrt{\rho_n}\,u_n\). The energy estimate bounds \(v_n\)
in \(L^\infty_tL^2_x\). The elementary inequality
\[
             |\sqrt a-\sqrt b|^4\le|a-b|^2,\qquad a,b\ge0,
\]
and \eqref{as:density} imply strong convergence of
\(\sqrt{\rho_n}\) in \(L^4(Q_T)\), hence in \(L^2_tL^4_x\).
Testing against smooth functions and using weak convergence of
\(u_n\) in \(L^2_tH^1_x\) identifies every weak \(L^2(Q_T)\)
limit of \(v_n\) as \(v=\sqrt\rho\,u\).

The duality in \eqref{as:momentum} is a Bochner-space duality
on the entire time interval. Therefore
\begin{equation}\label{as:norm-convergence}
\begin{aligned}
 \int_{Q_T}|v_n|^2\,\mathrm dx\,\mathrm dt
   &=\int_0^T\langle m_n,u_n\rangle_{H^{-3/5},H^{3/5}}\,\mathrm dt\\
   &\longrightarrow
       \int_0^T\langle m,u\rangle_{H^{-3/5},H^{3/5}}\,\mathrm dt
     =\int_{Q_T}|v|^2\,\mathrm dx\,\mathrm dt.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Indeed, the pairing with \(m_n-m\) tends to zero by strong
convergence and boundedness of \(u_n\); the pairing of \(m\)
with \(u_n-u\) tends to zero by weak convergence.
No nonsmooth endpoint test in the momentum equation is used.
Weak convergence and convergence of Hilbert norms prove
\eqref{as:weighted-strong}. Interpolation with the uniform
\(L^\infty_tL^2_x\) bound gives every finite time exponent.
Finally \(v_n\otimes v_n\to v\otimes v\) in \(L^1\).

label: ws:relative-theorem
title: Proposition
head: environment
name: Augmented relative stability

label: ws:bulk-absorption
title: Proof
body_md:
Add the integrated identity \eqref{ws:beta-relative-identity}
to \eqref{ws:physical-relative}. The two bulk differences combine as
\[
             -\int_{\mathbb T^2}(\rho^\beta-r^\beta)(D_U+1)\operatorname{div} w\,\mathrm dx.
\]
By \eqref{ws:pointwise} and weighted Young,
\begin{equation}\label{ws:bulk-absorption}
\begin{aligned}
 \left|\int_{\mathbb T^2}(\rho^\beta-r^\beta)(D_U+1)\operatorname{div} w\,\mathrm dx\right|
 \le{}&\varepsilon\int_{\mathbb T^2}(\mu+\rho^\beta)|\operatorname{div} w|^2\,\mathrm dx\\
 &+C_\varepsilon(1+\lVert D_U\rVert_\infty^2)\mathcal F.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Use \eqref{ws:density-force} with
\(G=F_{\rm ref}+\nabla r^\beta/r\), and use
\eqref{ws:magnetic-cross-bound} for the magnetic cross term.
The remaining convective, relative-pressure, augmented-potential,
and \(\mathbb M(Z)\) terms are bounded by
\(C\lVert \nabla U\rVert_\infty\mathcal F\).
Choose the finitely many Young constants with total cost at
most half of \(\mathcal D\). This proves
\eqref{ws:relative-estimate}, with
\begin{equation}\label{ws:comparison-coefficient}
\begin{aligned}
 G_T(t)=C\bigl[1+\lVert \nabla U\rVert_\infty+\lVert D_U\rVert_\infty^2
       +\lVert F_{\rm ref}\rVert_4^2
       +\lVert \nabla r\rVert_4^2+\lVert \nabla B\rVert_4^2\bigr].
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
The coefficient outside the brackets depends on fixed weak
density moments and the reference positive interval.
The comparison regularity gives
\[
 \nabla U\in L^2L^\infty,\qquad
 F_{\rm ref}\in L^2H^1\subset L^2L^4,\qquad
 \nabla r,\nabla B\in L^\infty L^4.
\]
The first inclusion follows from \(U\in L^2H^3\), not from
a false embedding \(H^2\subset W^{1,\infty}\). The force
bound follows from \eqref{ws:reference-force} or directly
from the stresses. Hence \(G_T\in L^1(0,T)\), including
at the initial time, and Gronwall gives \eqref{ws:gronwall}.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Common initial data give \(\mathcal F(0)=0\).
Proposition~\ref{ws:relative-theorem} implies
\(\mathcal F(t)=0\) for every \(t\in[0,T]\).
Strict convexity gives \(\rho=r\); the magnetic term gives
\(H=B\); and \(r\ge c_T>0\) then gives \(u=U\) almost
everywhere. Density, momentum, and magnetic field agree in
their canonical time representatives. The argument applies
on every finite interval on which the positive strong
reference exists.
head: environment

label: ws:scope
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{ws:scope}
The argument applies to every fixed \(\beta>1\), with no upper
restriction, and does not require \(\gamma\ge\beta\). Its constants
may depend on \(\beta\); no uniformity as \(\beta\to\infty\) is claimed.
This is uniqueness relative to the positive strong class
\eqref{ws:strong-class}, not uniqueness of arbitrary weak
solutions. The weaker assumptions \eqref{eq:data} do not
alone imply that a local strong solution has this comparison
regularity at time zero. In the large-background regime proved
below, the strong solution has the stated regularity on every
finite interval and therefore agrees with every weak solution
in the present class with common data. Weak--strong uniqueness
is not used to construct or continue that strong solution.

label: sl:basic
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The relative pressure potential at the constant state \(m\) is
\[
 \mathcal P(\rho\mid m)=
 \frac{\rho^\gamma-m^\gamma-\gamma m^{\gamma-1}(\rho-m)}{\gamma-1}.
\]
On the indicated interval it is comparable to
\(m^{\gamma-2}|\rho-m|^2\). Thus \eqref{eq:scaled-data} gives
\[
 E_m(0):=\int\left(\tfrac12\rho_0|u_0|^2+
       \mathcal P(\rho_0\mid m)+\tfrac12|H_0|^2\right)\,\mathrm dx\le C_Rm.
\]
Mass conservation allows the same linear pressure subtraction in the
exact energy identity. Its dissipation is
\(\mu\|\omega\|_2^2+\int A d^2+\nu\|j\|_2^2\).
Since \(\rho\ge m/2\) and \(A\ge c m^\beta\), the stated estimates follow.
The scaled assumption also gives
\(\|\rho_0/m-1\|_{H^2}\le Rm^{(1-\gamma)/2}\), which justifies the
initial density interval for every fixed \(\gamma>1\).

label: sl:magnetic
title: Lemma
head: environment

label: sl:potential-bound
title: Proof
body_md:
Write \(H=\overline H+\nabla^\perp\phi\), with \(\langle \phi\rangle=0\).
The scalar potential satisfies
\[
 \phi_t+u\cdot\nabla\phi=\nu\Delta\phi-u\times\overline H+c(t),
 \qquad c(t)=\langle u\times\overline H\rangle-\langle d\phi\rangle.
\]
Testing with \(\phi\), and using its zero mean, gives
\[
 \tfrac12(\|\phi\|_2^2)'+\nu\|\nabla\phi\|_2^2
 =\tfrac12\int d\phi^2-\int\phi(u-\overline u)\times\overline H.
\]
The zero-mean two-dimensional interpolation inequality bounds the first
term by \(\nu\|\nabla\phi\|_2^2/2+C\|d\|_2^2\|\phi\|_2^2\).
The second is bounded using \(\sup\|u\|_2\le C_R\).
Poincare's inequality and variation of constants therefore imply
\begin{equation}\label{sl:potential-bound}
 \sup\|\phi\|_2^2\le
 C_R\exp\left(C\int_0^T\|d\|_2^2\,\mathrm dt\right)\le C_R.
\end{equation}
In particular this first magnetic bound does not depend on \(V\).

For clarity, the exact current equation can be written
\[
 D_tj=H\cdot\nabla\omega-dj-\nabla d\times H+\mathcal T+\nu\Delta j,
\]
where
\[
 \mathcal T=\sum_{k=1}^2
 (\partial_1H_k\partial_ku_2-\partial_2H_k\partial_ku_1
 -\partial_1u_k\partial_kH_2+\partial_2u_k\partial_kH_1),
 \qquad |\mathcal T|\le C|\nabla u||\nabla H|.
\]
Testing with \(j\), then integrating the \(\nabla d\) term by parts,
gives
\begin{equation}\label{sl:current-identity}
 \tfrac12(\|j\|_2^2)'+\nu\|\nabla j\|_2^2
 =-\int\omega H\cdot\nabla j+\int j\mathcal T
        +\tfrac12\int dj^2+\int d(\nabla j\times H).
\end{equation}
Let \(U=\|\nabla u\|_2\), \(J=\|j\|_2\), and
\(J_1=\|\nabla j\|_2\). If \(K\ge1\) bounds \(\|\phi\|_2\),
Fourier interpolation gives
\[
 J\le CK^{1/3}J_1^{2/3},\qquad
 \|H-\overline H\|_\infty\le CK^{1/3}J_1^{2/3}.
\]
For the second estimate, split \(\nabla\phi\) at frequency \(N\):
its low and high parts are bounded by \(CN^2\|\phi\|_2\) and
\(CN^{-1}J_1\), respectively, and optimize. The right side of
\eqref{sl:current-identity} is at most
\(CUJJ_1+CU\|H\|_\infty J_1\). Young's inequality yields
\begin{equation}\label{sl:current-ode}
 (J^2)'+\nu J_1^2\le C_R(U^6+U^2).
\end{equation}
Because \(J_1^2\ge c_RJ^3\), scalar comparison gives
\(\sup J^2\le C_R(1+V^2)\). Integration, using
\(\int U^6\le V^2\int U^2\le C_RV^2m\), proves the first line of
\eqref{sl:magnetic-bounds}.

The endpoint \(H^1\hookrightarrow L^\infty\) is not used. Instead write
\[
 H-\overline H=e^{\nu t\Delta}(H_0-\overline H)
  +\int_0^t e^{\nu(t-s)\Delta}\operatorname{div}(u\otimes H-H\otimes u)(s)\,\mathrm d s.
\]
For fixed \(0<\varepsilon<1\), Sobolev multiplication gives
\(\|fg\|_{H^{1-\varepsilon/2}}\le
C_\varepsilon\|f\|_{H^1}\|g\|_{H^1}\). The mean-zero heat estimate is
\[
 \|e^{\nu t\Delta}\operatorname{div} F\|_{H^{2-\varepsilon}}
 \le C_{\varepsilon,\nu}(1+t^{-1+\varepsilon/4})e^{-c\nu t}
                         \|F\|_{H^{1-\varepsilon/2}}.
\]
This time kernel is integrable on \((0,\infty)\). It proves the
nonendpoint bound in \eqref{sl:magnetic-bounds}; choosing
\(\varepsilon=1/2\) gives explicitly
\(\sup\|H\|_\infty^2\le C_R(1+V^3)\).
Choosing \(\varepsilon<2/p\) also bounds \(j\) and hence \(K_H\) in
every fixed finite \(L^p\).

The time budgets follow without integrating a nonzero spatial mean:
\[
 \|K_H\|_2^2\le\|H\|_\infty^2J^2,\quad
 \|j\|_4^4\le CJ^2J_1^2,\quad
 \|\nabla K_H\|_2^2\le C\|H\|_\infty^2J_1^2+C\|j\|_4^4.
\]
These and \eqref{sl:basic-budgets} give the quadratic, derivative and
fourth-power budgets. Finally
\(\|K_H\|_4^2\le C\|K_H\|_2(\|K_H\|_2+\|\nabla K_H\|_2)\)
and Cauchy--Schwarz give the remaining term.

label: sl:low-acoustic
title: Lemma
head: environment

label: sl:acoustic-identity
title: Proof
body_md:
Set \(c_0=D^{-1}\), \(Q=c_0A\gamma\rho^{\gamma-1}\), and
\[
 \mathcal A_0=\tfrac12\int(c_0Ad^2+Q|q|^2),\quad
 \mathscr D_0=c_0\int b|\nabla S|^2,\quad
 \Lambda(\rho)=2\mu\log\rho+\rho^\beta/\beta.
\]
Direct testing of the momentum and differentiated mass equations gives
\begin{equation}\label{sl:acoustic-identity}
\begin{aligned}
 \mathcal A_0'+\mathscr D_0={}&\mathcal R_q
 -c_0\mu\int b\nabla S\cdot\nabla^\perp\omega
 -c_0\int b\nabla S\cdot K_H+2c_0\int S\det\nabla u\\
 &-\tfrac{c_0}{2}\int(A+\beta\rho^\beta)d^3,\qquad
 \mathcal R_q=-\int Qq\cdot(\nabla u)^{\mathsf T}q
   +\tfrac12\int Q(\sigma+2-\gamma)d|q|^2.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Here \(D_tq=-\nabla d-(\nabla u)^{\mathsf T}q\) and
\(D_t\Lambda=-S\); these also give the exact corrector identity
\begin{equation}\label{sl:corrector-identity}
\begin{aligned}
 c_0\left(\int y d\right)'={}&-c_0\int Ad^2
  -c_0\int(A/\rho)q\cdot\nabla S+\int Q|q|^2\\
 &-c_0\int(A/\rho)q\cdot K_H+2c_0\int y\det\nabla u,
 \qquad y=\Lambda-\langle \Lambda\rangle.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Indeed \(D_td=\operatorname{div} D_tu-\operatorname{tr}((\nabla u)^2)\), and
\(d^2-\operatorname{tr}((\nabla u)^2)=2\det\nabla u\).
The shear pairing in \eqref{sl:corrector-identity} is zero because
\((A/\rho)q\) is a scalar gradient. Also
\(\int\det\nabla u=0\), so subtracting \(\langle \Lambda\rangle\) introduces no term.

Choose a fixed sufficiently small \(\varepsilon_0>0\), and put
\[
 \eta=\varepsilon_0\mathfrak d,\qquad
 X=\mathcal A_0-\eta c_0\int yd.
\]
Since \(\mathfrak d^2\le c_s^2\), Poincare gives
\[
 \left|\eta c_0\int yd\right|
 \le C\eta m\|q\|_2\|d\|_2
 \le C\varepsilon_0
             \bigl(m\|d\|_2^2+m^\gamma\|q\|_2^2\bigr).
\]
Hence \(X\asymp\mathcal A_0\), with equivalence constants independent
of the bootstrap heights. The weighted mean constraint \(\int S/A=0\) implies
\(\|d\|_2\le Cm^{-\beta}\|\nabla S\|_2\).
Inserting minus \(\eta\) times \eqref{sl:corrector-identity} into
\eqref{sl:acoustic-identity}, the two quadratic corrector errors are
absorbed using
\[
 \eta c_0\int Ad^2\le C\varepsilon_0\mathscr D_0,\qquad
 \eta c_0\left|\int(A/\rho)q\cdot\nabla S\right|
 \le\epsilon\mathscr D_0+C_\epsilon\eta^2m^\beta\|q\|_2^2.
\]
The first absorption uses \(\eta/D\le\varepsilon_0\), and the
second uses \(\eta/\Gamma\le\varepsilon_0\):
\(C_\epsilon\eta^2m^\beta\|q\|_2^2\) is a small multiple of
\(\eta\int Q|q|^2\).
The remaining flux dissipation controls
\(\mathfrak d\,m\|d\|_2^2\), because
\(\mathscr D_0\ge cD\,m\|d\|_2^2\) and \(\mathfrak d\le D\).

For completeness the other costs, with \(U=\|\nabla u\|_2\) and
\(\delta_\rho=\|\rho/m-1\|_\infty\), are
\begin{align}
 \left|2c_0\int S\det\nabla u\right|
 &\le\epsilon\mathscr D_0+C_\epsilon m^{2-\beta}U^4,
                                                        \label{sl:low-wente}\\
 \left|2\eta c_0\int y\det\nabla u\right|
 &\le\epsilon\eta m^\gamma\|q\|_2^2
                       +C_\epsilon\eta m^{2-\gamma}U^4,\notag\\
 c_0\mu\left|\int b\nabla S\cdot\nabla^\perp\omega\right|
 &\le\epsilon\mathscr D_0+
             C_\epsilon\delta_\rho^2m^{-\beta}\|\nabla\omega\|_2^2,
                                                        \notag\\
 \tfrac{c_0}{2}\left|\int(A+\beta\rho^\beta)d^3\right|
 &\le\epsilon\mathscr D_0+C_\epsilon m^{2-\beta}\|d\|_2^4.
                                                        \notag
\end{align}
For the last inequality, $\int d=\int S/A=0$ and
$\nabla d=A^{-1}\nabla S-\sigma dq$ give, by Poincare and
$H^1\hookrightarrow L^4$,
\[
 \|d\|_{H^1}\le C m^{-\beta}\|\nabla S\|_2
                  +C\|q\|_4\|d\|_{H^1}
             \le C m^{-\beta}\|\nabla S\|_2,
\]
where the small $\|q\|_4$ term is absorbed using
\eqref{sl:low-inputs}. The first two inequalities are periodic Wente
duality. Their remainders
are both at most \(C_\epsilon(m/\mathfrak d)U^4\), since
\[
 m^{2-\beta}\le C m/\mathfrak d,\qquad
 \eta m^{2-\gamma}\le C m/\mathfrak d.
\]
The latter follows from \(\mathfrak d^2\le c_s^2\).
The shear term
uses \(\int\nabla S\cdot\nabla^\perp\omega=0\), subtracting the
constant \(m^{-1}\) from \(b\). Both magnetic pairings cost
\(\epsilon\mathscr D_0+\epsilon\eta m^\gamma\|q\|_2^2+
C_\epsilon m^{-\beta}\|K_H\|_2^2\).
For the corrector magnetic pairing this uses
\(\eta m^{-\gamma}\le C m^{-\beta}\), which follows from
\(\eta\le\varepsilon_0\Gamma\).
The cubic divergence remainder is absorbable: its ratio to
\(\mathscr D_0\) is at most \(C V m^{2-2\beta}=o(1)\).

If \(\ell=\log\rho-\langle \log\rho\rangle\), then
\(\rho/m=e^\ell/\langle e^\ell\rangle\). Sobolev embedding and
\eqref{sl:low-inputs} show
\(\delta_\rho^2\le C\|q\|_{H^1}^2\le CMm^{1-\gamma}\).
Finally the unestimated density strain satisfies
\[
 |\mathcal R_q|\le Cm^\gamma U\|q\|_4^2
 \le CU X^{1/2}(Mm)^{1/2}
 \le\epsilon\mathfrak d X+C_\epsilon M\frac m{\mathfrak d}U^2.
\]
Together with \(U^4\le VU^2\), these estimates prove
\eqref{sl:low-differential}.

The scaled data give \(X(0)\le C_Rm\). Variation of constants, using
the velocity supremum for the first source and the magnetic and
vorticity integrals for the others, yields
\[
 X(t)\le C_Rm e^{-c\mathfrak d t}
 +C_*\left(\frac m{\mathfrak d^2}
                   +m^{1-\beta}+m^{2-\gamma-\beta}\right).
\]
The last term is smaller than \(m^{1-\beta}\), since \(\gamma>1\).
This proves \eqref{sl:low-profile}; it is not necessary to discard
the magnetic tail \(m^{1-\beta}\).
Integrating \eqref{sl:low-differential} and using
\(\int U^2\le C_Rm\) gives
\[
 \int_0^T\|\nabla S\|_2^2\,\mathrm dt
 \le C_*\left(m^{\beta+1}+\frac{m^{\beta+2}}{\mathfrak d}
                                  +m+m^{2-\gamma}\right).
\]
The last two terms are bounded by \(m^{\beta+1}\), proving the
first estimate in \eqref{sl:flux-budgets}.
When \(\beta>2\), the inequality \(s>1\) makes
\(m^{\beta+2}/\mathfrak d\le C m^{\beta+1}\); for
\(\beta\le2\), this term is comparable to \(m^3\).
To obtain the exponentially weighted estimate, multiply by
\(e^{-\zeta\mathfrak d t}\). Integration by parts gives
\[
 \int_0^T e^{-\zeta\mathfrak d t}X'\,\mathrm dt
 =e^{-\zeta\mathfrak d T}X(T)-X(0)
       +\zeta\mathfrak d\int_0^T e^{-\zeta\mathfrak d t}X\,\mathrm dt.
\]
The velocity source now costs only \(C_*m/\mathfrak d^2\), and
the other source terms retain their preceding global budgets.
Since \(\mathfrak d\to\infty\), their sum and \(X(0)\) are at most
\(C_{*,\zeta}m\). Multiplication by \(m^\beta\) proves the second
estimate in \eqref{sl:flux-budgets}.

label: sl:mixed
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{sl:mixed}
Assume the density interval, \(\sup\|u\|_{H^1}^2\le V\), and
\(\sup\|q\|_{H^1}^2\le Mm^{1-\gamma}\). Define
\[
 g=m^2/\rho^2,\qquad
 \mathcal E=\tfrac12\int\left((m^2/\rho)\omega^2+j^2\right),\qquad
 \mathcal B_S(T)=m^{-1}\int_0^T\delta_\rho(t)^2\|\nabla S\|_2^2\,\mathrm dt.
\]
For sufficiently large \(m\), depending on the fixed heights,
\begin{equation}\label{sl:mixed-bound}
 \sup_{t\le T}\frac{\mathcal E(t)}m+
 \frac1m\int_0^T(\mu\|\nabla\omega\|_2^2+\nu\|\nabla j\|_2^2)\,\mathrm dt
 \le C_R\left[1+\mathcal B_S(T)+(1+V^3)m^{-\beta}\right].
\end{equation}
In particular the principal constant on the right does not depend on
\(V\) or \(M\).
head: environment

label: sl:mixed-identity
title: Proof
body_md:
The normalized potential vorticity \(z=m\omega/\rho\) obeys the
mass-weighted cancellation of compression. Combining its quadratic
energy with \eqref{sl:current-identity} gives the exact identity
\begin{equation}\label{sl:mixed-identity}
\begin{aligned}
 \mathcal E'+\mu\int g|\nabla\omega|^2+\nu\|\nabla j\|_2^2
 ={}&-\tfrac\mu2\int\omega\nabla g\cdot\nabla\omega
       -\tfrac12\int(g-1)J(\omega,S)\\
 &+\tfrac12\int(g-1)
           [\omega H\cdot\nabla j-jH\cdot\nabla\omega]\\
 &+\int j\mathcal T+\tfrac12\int dj^2+
                                     \int d(\nabla j\times H),
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
where \(J(f,g)=\nabla f\times\nabla g\).
To verify the two less immediate cancellations, the vorticity equation is
\[
 D_t\omega+d\omega=\mu\operatorname{div}(b\nabla\omega)
                  -bq\times\nabla S+\operatorname{curl}(bK_H).
\]
Since \(\nabla g=-2gq\), its scalar coupling is
\(-\tfrac12\int(g-1)J(\omega,S)\). Pressure contributes zero because
\(g\) and \(\rho^\gamma\) are functions of the same density.
Its magnetic contribution is
\(\tfrac12\int g[\omega H\cdot\nabla j-jH\cdot\nabla\omega]\);
the part with \(g=1\) cancels the first term of
\eqref{sl:current-identity}. Thus \eqref{sl:mixed-identity} does not
discard a principal Lorentz coupling.

Put \(X_\omega=\|\nabla\omega\|_2\), \(J=\|j\|_2\), and
\(J_1=\|\nabla j\|_2\). Since \(\omega,j\) have zero mean, the first
and the residual magnetic terms in \eqref{sl:mixed-identity} are bounded by
\[
 C\mu\|q\|_4X_\omega^2,\qquad
 C\delta_\rho\|H\|_\infty X_\omega J_1,
\]
and are absorbed for large \(m\). The baroclinic term costs
\(\epsilon\mu X_\omega^2+C_R\delta_\rho^2\|\nabla S\|_2^2\).
The stretching term is estimated without inserting the velocity
bootstrap into its rotational part:
\begin{equation}\label{sl:stretching-principal}
\begin{aligned}
 \left|\int j\mathcal T\right|
 &\le C\|\nabla u\|_2\|j\|_4\|\nabla H\|_4
 \le\epsilon\nu J_1^2+C_RJ^2(\|\omega\|_2^2+\|d\|_2^2)\\
 &\le\epsilon\nu J_1^2+\frac{C_R}{m}J^2\mathcal E
                          +C_R(1+V^2)\|d\|_2^2.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
The last two compression terms of \eqref{sl:mixed-identity} cost
\(\epsilon\nu J_1^2+C_R(1+V^3)\|d\|_2^2\).
Consequently
\[
 \mathcal E'+c(\mu X_\omega^2+\nu J_1^2)
 \le\frac{C_R}{m}J^2\mathcal E
       +C_R\delta_\rho^2\|\nabla S\|_2^2
       +C_R(1+V^3)\|d\|_2^2.
\]
The Gronwall exponent is bounded by the basic energy alone:
\(m^{-1}\int J^2\le C_R\), independently of \(V\).
Also \(\mathcal E(0)\le C_Rm\) and
\(m^{-1}\int\|d\|_2^2\le C_Rm^{-\beta}\).
Gronwall followed by integration proves \eqref{sl:mixed-bound}.

label: sl:finite-p
title: Lemma
head: environment

label: sl:finite-p-test
title: Proof
body_md:
Set \(\varrho=\rho/m\) and \(z=\omega/\varrho\). The exact equation is
\[
 \varrho D_tz=\frac\mu m\operatorname{div}(\nabla z+qz)
       -\frac1{m\varrho}q\times\nabla S
       +\frac1m\operatorname{curl}(K_H/\varrho).
\]
Let \(E_p=p^{-1}\int\varrho|z|^p\),
\(Z_p=\operatorname{sgn}(z)|z|^{p/2}\), and
\(D_p=\|\nabla Z_p\|_2\). The mass equation cancels all compression
reaction terms in the test, giving
\begin{equation}\label{sl:finite-p-test}
\begin{aligned}
 E_p'+\frac{4\mu(p-1)}{mp^2}D_p^2
 ={}&-\frac{2\mu(p-1)}{mp}\int q\cdot Z_p\nabla Z_p
 -\frac1m\int\varrho^{-1}(q\times\nabla S)|z|^{p-2}z\\
 &-\frac{p-1}{m}\int\varrho^{-1}K_H\cdot\nabla^\perp z\,|z|^{p-2}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
The needed Poincare inequality is not based on a false zero mean for
\(z\). Rather \(\int\varrho z=\int\omega=0\). The map
\(\Psi(s)=\operatorname{sgn}(s)|s|^{2/p}\) is \(2/p\)-Holder, so
\[
 |\Psi(\langle Z_p\rangle)|\int\varrho
 \le C_p\int\varrho|Z_p-\langle Z_p\rangle|^{2/p}.
\]
Ordinary Poincare then gives
\(\|Z_p\|_2\le C_pD_p\), and for every fixed finite \(a\ge2\),
\(\|Z_p\|_a\le C_{p,a}\|Z_p\|_2^{2/a}D_p^{1-2/a}\).
The first term of \eqref{sl:finite-p-test} is at most
\(C_{p,r}Q_rD_p^2/m\), and is absorbed. The magnetic term is bounded by
\(\epsilon D_p^2/m+C_{p,\epsilon}B_p^2E_p^{1-2/p}/m\), and hence
by another small part of the Poincare damping plus \(C_pB_p^p/m\).

For the scalar forcing define
\[
 t_*=1-2/p+2/r\in(0,1),\quad a_*=1/2-1/r,\quad
 k_*=\frac{2}{2-t_*}\in(1,2).
\]
Holder and the preceding interpolation give
\[
 |R_S|\le\frac{C_{p,r}}m Q_rG E_p^{a_*}D_p^{t_*}
 \le\frac\epsilon mD_p^2+\frac{C_{p,r}}m(Q_rG)^{k_*}
                                            E_p^{1-k_*/p},
\]
where \(a_*k_*=1-k_*/p\). Thus
\[
 E_p'+\frac cmE_p\le\frac Cm(Q_rG)^{k_*}E_p^{1-k_*/p}
                          +\frac CmB_p^p.
\]
Apply the chain rule to \((E_p+B_p^p)^{k_*/p}\); zero values can be
handled by a positive regularization. The resulting linear inequality
has source \(C[(Q_rG)^{k_*}+B_p^{k_*}]/m\).
Variation of constants and Holder's inequality with \(k_*<2\) give
\[
 \frac1m\int_0^t e^{-c(t-s)/m}(Q_rG)^{k_*}(s)\,\mathrm d s
 \le C\left(\frac1m\int_0^t
              e^{-c(t-s)/m}Q_r(s)^2G(s)^2\,\mathrm d s\right)^{k_*/2}.
\]
Since \(E_p^{1/p}\asymp\|\omega\|_p\), this proves
\eqref{sl:finite-p-bound}. The actual shear time scale \(m\) has been
retained throughout.

title: Proof
body_md:
The mass normalization used above and the finite Sobolev embeddings give
\(\delta_\rho^2+\|q\|_r^2\le C_r\|q\|_{H^1}^2\).
Write \(G=\|\nabla S\|_2\). First let \(1<\beta\le2\) and set
\(T_0=\min\{T,t_L\}\). Integrate \eqref{sl:low-differential} only
over \([0,T_0]\), using \(X(0)\le C_Rm\), \(X(T_0)\ge0\),
\(\sup\|\nabla u\|_2^2\le V\), the magnetic budget
\(\int\|K_H\|_2^2\,\mathrm dt\le C_{R,V}m\), and the coarse mixed bound
\(\int\|\nabla\omega\|_2^2\,\mathrm dt\le Lm\). Since
\(\mathfrak d=D\asymp m^{\beta-1}\), this gives
\begin{equation}\label{sl:initial-layer-flux}
\begin{aligned}
 \int_0^{T_0}G^2\,\mathrm dt
 &\le C_*\left(m^{\beta+1}+m^2t_L+m+m^{2-\gamma}\right)\\
 &\le C_*\left(m^{\beta+1}+m^{3-\beta}\log m
                           +m+m^{2-\gamma}\right)
 \le C_*m^{\beta+1}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
In the last inequality,
\(m^{3-\beta}\log m=o(m^{\beta+1})\) because \(\beta>1\),
while \(\gamma>\beta+1\). This prefix estimate does not presume
existence up to \(t_L\).

Use \(\|q\|_{H^1}^2\le Mm^{1-\gamma}\) on the prefix. On
\([t_L,T]\), when nonempty, use \eqref{sl:staged-profile-input}
and the full-time budget \(\int_0^TG^2\,\mathrm dt\le C_*m^3\) from
\eqref{sl:flux-budgets}. Thus
\[
 \frac1m\int_0^T(\delta_\rho^2+\|q\|_r^2)G^2\,\mathrm dt
 \le C_{r,*}\left(m^{\beta+1-\gamma}
                             +m^{a_*+2-\gamma}\right).
\]
Both exponents are strictly negative. Importantly, the full-time
\(m^3\) budget has only been paired with the improved tail bound,
not with the coarse initial-layer bound.

For \(\beta>2\), multiply \eqref{sl:profile-input} by \(G^2/m\)
and apply separately the weighted and unweighted estimates in
\eqref{sl:flux-budgets}. Their contributions are respectively
\(C_{r,*}m^{\beta+1-\gamma}\) and
\(C_{r,*}m^{\beta+2-s-\gamma}\). Writing
\(a=\gamma-\beta>1\) makes the
two exponents \(1-a<0\) and \(2-s-a<0\), since \(s>1\).
This proves \eqref{sl:feedback-budget} in both branches.

Now apply Lemma~\ref{sl:mixed}, \eqref{sl:low-profile}, the Hodge identity
\(\|\nabla u\|_2^2=\|d\|_2^2+\|\omega\|_2^2\), and the basic kinetic
bound. Lemmas~\ref{sl:magnetic} and~\ref{sl:finite-p} give the last
assertion, replacing the history integral by the larger full integral
in \eqref{sl:feedback-budget}. The smallness assumption of
Lemma~\ref{sl:finite-p} follows already from the coarse bound
\(\|q\|_{H^1}^2\le Mm^{1-\gamma}\).
All dependence on the high bootstrap heights is multiplied by a
strictly negative power of \(m\). Thus these implications do not
introduce a constant-level circular dependence.

\label{sg:full-time-remark}
In this conditional remark the constants are denoted by $C_*$;
they become data-dependent constants $C_R$ after the bootstrap heights
are fixed in Section~\ref{sec:strong-closure}.
Suppose the lower-order bootstrap has additionally supplied
\[
 \int_0^T\|\nabla\omega\|_2^2\,\mathrm dt\le C_Rm.
\]
Then, on any interval \([s,T]\) on which the improved input and
weight conditions of Proposition~\ref{sg:high-proposition} hold,
the sharp inequality \eqref{sg:joint-sharp}, rather than
its constant-source simplification, yields
\[
 \int_s^T
       (\mathscr D_S+\mathscr B_\rho+m^{-h}Z^2)\,\mathrm dt
                         \le C\,Y_h(s)+C_*m^{3-\beta}.
\]
In particular this is bounded by \(C_*m^{3-\beta}\) whenever
\(Y_h(s)\le C_*m\), since \(\beta\le2\). This includes the first
stage starting at zero, with \(Y_h(0)\le C_Rm\).
Indeed
\(\int\|\omega\|_4^4\le
C\sup\|\omega\|_2^2\int\|\nabla\omega\|_2^2\le C_*m\),
while
\(\int\|d\|_4^4\le
C\sup\|d\|_{H^1}^2\int\|d\|_2^2\le C_*m^{1-\beta}\).
Hodge gives \(\int\|\nabla u\|_4^4\le C_*m\).
The transport remainder costs \(m^{\kappa_P+1-h}\),
which is smaller than \(m^{3-\beta}\) by
\eqref{sg:exponent-choices}; the compression remainders
cost \(m^{3-h-\beta}+m^{e_P+1-\beta}\), also smaller.
One must not obtain this conclusion by integrating the
constant source in \eqref{sg:joint-simplified}.

label: sg:super-coercivity
title: Proof
body_md:
We retain the exact symbols in \eqref{sg:frequency-parameters},
rather than replacing the multiplier by a scalar. At every nonzero
torus frequency,
\begin{equation}\label{sg:super-coercivity}
 \alpha(\xi)\ge c\min\{D,\Gamma\}=c\mathfrak d,
 \qquad
 \mathscr D_S+\mathscr B_\rho
       \ge c\mathfrak d\mathcal A_1.
\end{equation}
The second statement follows from \eqref{sg:energy-equivalence} and
the Poincare inequality for \(f\); indeed the flux part has the
stronger rate \(D\ge\mathfrak d\). The multiplier bound
\(\alpha(\xi)\le c_s|\xi|/2\) and the density recovery
\eqref{sg:q-small} are unchanged, so the corrected energy remains
coercive with a fixed small \(\varepsilon_0\).

\emph{Acoustic errors and pressure positivity.}
Use the exact identities \eqref{sg:exact-high-identity} and
\eqref{sg:cross-identity}. The algebraic estimates
\eqref{sg:forcing-bound}--\eqref{sg:quadratic-density-strain},
\eqref{sg:commutator-budget}, and
\eqref{sg:diffusion-cross}--\eqref{sg:cross-physical} do not require
\(h>\beta\) or \(K\to\infty\). Their absorption now uses
\(\mathfrak d\), not \(D\). To make this change explicit, the
coefficients multiplying \(\mathcal A_1\), apart from the
differentiated solenoidal strain, are bounded by a fixed multiple of
\begin{equation}\label{sg:super-error-coefficients}
\begin{aligned}
 &m^{h-2\beta+1-2\gamma}+m^{-(\beta-1)/3}
       +m^{\beta-\gamma}+m^{-(\beta-1)/(p-1)}\\
 &\quad +m^{(h+1)/(p+1)}
       +m^{-(\beta-1)\theta/(2-\theta)}
       +m^{\beta+1-2\gamma}+m^{1-\beta}+B_q+B_q^2,
       \qquad \theta=2/p.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Each is \(o(\mathfrak d)\). For the only positive exponent that
needs a choice of \(p\), use \eqref{sg:super-exponents}. For the
shear term, \(h=2s\), \(s\le\beta-1\), and \(\gamma>\beta+1\)
give \(h-2\beta+1-2\gamma-s<0\). The diffusion cross term has
relative exponent \(\beta+1-2\gamma-s<0\). All the other displayed
coefficients either have negative powers or tend to zero by
\eqref{sg:q-small}.

The genuine pressure calculation
\eqref{sg:cross-pressure}--\eqref{sg:pressure-positive} remains
valid also when \(K\) tends to zero or stays bounded, because
\[
 (\delta_\rho+B_q)\sqrt{1+K^2}
       \le C_*(m^{(1-\gamma)/2}+m^{1-\beta})\longrightarrow0.
\]
In estimating the diffusion cross term, the coefficient left after
paying \(\mathscr B_\rho\) is exactly of order
\(\Gamma m^{-\gamma}\asymp m^{-\beta}\); hence it is paid by
\(\mathscr D_S\) regardless of the size of \(K\). The resolvent
commutator uses \(\Gamma/K=c_s\) and the bounds already displayed
before \eqref{sg:commutator-raw}, which hold for every \(K>0\).
The adverse inverse-viscosity cross terms contain
\(\delta_\rho K\) or \(B_qK\), both tending to zero by the same
estimate. Thus no fast acoustic gap has been assumed in this step.

\emph{Differentiated density strain without a cutoff.}
Let \(E_q=m^\gamma\|\nabla q\|_2^2\). For any of its principal
tensor contractions, the finite-exponent interpolation used in
\eqref{sg:high-density-estimate} gives directly
\[
 |\mathcal G|\le C_p\|\omega\|_p^{1/2}Z^{1/2}E_q.
\]
Here all density frequencies are retained. Twice applying Young's
inequality yields
\begin{equation}\label{sg:super-all-frequency}
\begin{aligned}
 |\mathcal G|
 &\le\delta\mathfrak d E_q
       +C_{\delta,p}\mathfrak d^{-1}\|\omega\|_p ZE_q
 \le\delta\mathscr B_\rho+\delta m^{-h}Z^2
       +C_{\delta,p}m^h\mathfrak d^{-2}\|\omega\|_p^2E_q^2.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Since \(E_q\le C_*m\), the last term divided by
\(\mathfrak d E_q\) is bounded by
\(C_*m^{h+1}\mathfrak d^{-3}\le C_*m^{1-s}=o(1)\).
The genuine coefficient \(B(\rho)\) is bounded in \(L^\infty\),
so this estimate includes the variable-coefficient principal
contractions. The cubic terms generated by
\(\nabla w=A(\nabla q+\sigma q\otimes q)\) are integrated once
against \(\nabla v\), exactly as in the calculation preceding
\eqref{sg:full-differentiated-strain}. They cost
\(C_p\|\omega\|_p(B_q+B_q^2)E_q=o(\mathfrak d)E_q\).
Combining these estimates proves
\begin{equation}\label{sg:super-acoustic}
\begin{aligned}
 \mathcal A_{\mathsf T}'+c\mathfrak d\mathcal A_{\mathsf T}
      +c\mathscr D_S+c\mathscr B_\rho
 \le{}&\delta m^{-h}Z^2+C_\delta m^{2-\beta}\|\nabla u\|_4^4
 +C_\delta m^{-\beta}
           (\|\nabla K_H\|_2^2+B_q^2\|K_H\|_4^2).
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

\emph{Palinstrophy, including the baroclinic term.}
Apply the original test \eqref{sg:palinstrophy-identity} with the
weight \(m^{1-h}\). The transport and compression estimates
\eqref{sg:pal-transport}--\eqref{sg:pal-compression} hold with the
present \(h,P\). The drift is bounded by
\[
 \delta m^{-h}Z^2+C_*m^{-h}\|q\|_8^4
 \le\delta m^{-h}Z^2
       +C_*m^{1-h-2\gamma-s}\mathscr B_\rho,
\]
using \(\|q\|_8^4\le C_*m^{1-\gamma}\|\nabla q\|_2^2\) and
\eqref{sg:super-coercivity}. Its last coefficient tends to zero.
For the baroclinic remainder retain the second line of
\eqref{sg:pal-baroclinic}, but pay its last term from the flux
dissipation, rather than from a putative rate \(D\) on the density:
\begin{equation}\label{sg:super-baroclinic}
\begin{aligned}
 m^{\beta-2h}\|q\|_4^4\|f\|_2^2
 &\le C_*m^{\beta-2h+2-2\gamma}\|f\|_2^2
 \le C_*m^{2-2h-2a}\mathscr D_S=o(\mathscr D_S).
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
This uses \(\|f\|_2\le C\|\nabla f\|_2\), and is valid even when
\(h\le\beta\). Finally \eqref{sg:pal-magnetic} gives its original
coefficient \(m^{-h}\). Adding these five remainder estimates to
\eqref{sg:super-acoustic} proves \eqref{sg:super-sharp}, with
\[
 \mathcal M=C_*(m^{-\beta}+m^{-h})
          (\|\nabla K_H\|_2^2+B_q^2\|K_H\|_4^2).
\]
The input \eqref{sg:lower-inputs} and \(B_q^2=o(1)\) imply
\eqref{sg:super-magnetic}. Neither of its two powers is discarded.

\emph{The dynamic estimate and the full-time budget.}
As before,
\(m^{-h}Z^2\ge c(V)m^{h-2}\mathcal V_h^2\). Completing the
square with the actual acoustic rate gives
\[
 c(V)m^{h-2}\mathcal V_h^2
       \ge c_1\mathfrak d\mathcal V_h
                         -C_*\mathfrak d^2m^{2-h}
       \ge c_1\mathfrak d\mathcal V_h-C_*m^2.
\]
The potential estimate \eqref{sg:potential-H1}, Hodge, and the
fixed finite-exponent vorticity bound give
\(\|\nabla u\|_4+\|d\|_2\le C_*\). Moreover
\(\kappa_P-h<0\), \(2-h<0\), and \(e_P\le2-h\).
Thus \eqref{sg:super-sharp} implies
\[
 Y'+c\mathfrak dY\le C_*m^2+\mathcal M.
\]
Variation of constants gives
\[
 Y(t)\le C_Rm e^{-c\mathfrak d t}
       +C_*(m^{2-s}+m^{1-\beta}+m^{1-h}).
\]
Both magnetic powers are at most \(2-s\), since
\(s\le\beta-1\) and \(h=2s\). This proves the first estimate in
\eqref{sg:super-dynamic}; \eqref{sg:q-small} gives the second.

For the full-time estimate, do not integrate the constant source
\(m^2\). The additional lower-order budget, Hodge, and
\eqref{sg:potential-H1} give
\(\int\|\nabla u\|_4^4\,\mathrm dt\le C_*m\), exactly by the two
interpolations in Remark~\ref{sg:full-time-remark}. Also
\(\int\|\nabla u\|_2^{\kappa_P}\,\mathrm dt\le C_*m\).
Integrating \eqref{sg:super-sharp}, including its initial energy,
therefore costs at most a fixed multiple of
\[
 m+m^{3-\beta}+m^{\kappa_P+1-h}
       +m^{3-h-\beta}+m^{e_P+1-\beta}
       +m^{1-\beta}+m^{1-h}\le C m.
\]
Here \(\beta>2\), \(h>2\), and \(\kappa_P<h\) are precisely
the inequalities needed for the last comparison. This proves
\eqref{sg:super-full-time}.
